title: Load a slide into a microscope's stage by its edges: coverslip up, seated under the objective, spring arm lowered gently
instruction: Load the prepared slide into the microscope's slide holder, coverslip up and seated against the holder's back edge and jaw, so the specimen is under the objective. Handle the slide only by its edges and label end.
context: Every look at a slide in research, teaching and clinical labs starts with this step. AmScope's manual: "pushing the caliper lever outward to open the caliper, then sliding the slide in place so the long edge is flush against the back edge of the template. Gently releasing the caliper will secure the slide in place." Olympus CX23: lower the stage, slide it in "from front toward back"; "If you return the holding lever c with excess force or release your hand from the holding lever knob b in the middle, the lever may collide with the specimen slide to damage it." Carolina: "held by the edges, avoiding the cover glass area." For a parallel gripper the hard parts are holding a 1 mm glass plate only by its edges or label end while turning it from standing to flat, and pushing it into the holder. Unlike clamp loading, the seat is under the objective, so the slide is set down in front and pushed in by its 1 mm edge; the arm is lowered onto glass.
setup: Positions in mm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table. Table: the station's wooden bench top. Microscope: AmScope M620 (40X-1000X; monocular, about US$219) or AmScope B120C (binocular, about US$300; the one modelled), the same stand with a different head: two-layer mechanical stage 116 x 125 mm with 70 x 25 mm X-Y travel as modelled (AmScope's current pages list 127 x 118 mm and 70 x 21 mm), slide holder (a metal template) with a back edge and fixed jaw on the left and a spring caliper on the right (a curved arm swinging in the stage plane, its tip pressing the slide's right end toward the jaw, its lever knob at the stage's right edge). Powered off, head toward the robot, optical axis at x 360, y 0. It is fixed to the table by two 25 x 100 mm strips of double-sided foam mounting tape under its base, or a padded bench clamp on the base's rear lip. The stage is fully lowered (top about 190 mm up; measured on the unit before the trials, by the README's method) with the 4x objective in the path, its X and Y scales at the recorded readings that put a seated slide's centre on the optical axis; the caliper is closed. Bench slide holder: Heathrow Scientific HS15981C (white polyethylene, 15 angled slots, 152 x 102 x 20 mm), centred at x 300, y 220, its long side along y so the slots run front to back. Slide: a standard prepared slide made to the README's recipe: a ground-edge colour-frosted soda-lime slide (75 x 25 x 1 mm, about 5 g, frosted end about 20 mm) with a 22 mm square cover glass (0.13-0.17 mm) centred within 1 mm over a dried drop of methylene blue in permanent mountant. It stands alone in the holder's middle slot, label end up, coverslip facing the microscope (-y); the neighbouring slots are empty. Protected area: both faces outside the frosted label end, and the coverslip. Once seated, the label end may lie at either end. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: 0 at any time if: a gripper touches the coverslip or a face of the slide outside the label end (while holding, the logged gripper opening is under 5 mm, a pinch across the faces, and the pads are not wholly on the label end; or, in the side video, a pad rests on the top face outside the label end or on the coverslip); the slide or coverslip is cracked or chipped (inspected after the trial); a gripper or the slide touches an objective; the slide drops (free fall over 10 mm) or rests anywhere but the holder, a gripper or the stage; the stage's X or Y reading changes by more than 1 mm. Hard landing (caps at 0.75): take the arm's final landing (it comes to rest on the slide after the hand lets go; a touch while a hand holds the arm open does not count): the tip's mean speed over its last 5 mm before it stops exceeds V_max (20 mm/s, or the value measured by the README's method: at 60 fps, fewer than 15 frames), or no gripper was on the caliper (lever or arm) when the tip met the slide on that approach. From the final 1 s, both grippers 3 cm or more from slide, caliper and lever: 0.25: the slide lies flat on the stage (0.3 mm feeler does not enter under any corner), coverslip up; 0.5: also the caliper's tip rests on it; 0.75: also seated (0.3 mm feeler does not enter at the back edge's two ends or at the jaw), with a hard landing; 1.0: the same with a gentle landing. Coverslip down, slide riding on the template, or nothing done: 0. Real trial: feeler gauge, the stage's own scales, the logged gripper opening, an overhead 60 fps video with a 1 mm tick strip along the tip's path, and a side video at stage height. Under the objective: the coverslip is centred and the stage starts at its centred readings, so a seated slide on an unmoved stage is under the objective.
reset_notes: Push the caliper lever out and slide the slide forward by its front edge until it overhangs the stage; take it by its long edges and stand it back in the middle slot, label up, coverslip toward the microscope; release the caliper gently; reset the X and Y scales, lower the stage and turn the 4x into the path. Wipe the slide with lens tissue if marked; replace it from the spares if cracked or chipped. If glass breaks: put on cut-resistant gloves, pick up the pieces with tweezers or a dustpan and brush (never bare fingers or the grippers), put them in a broken-glass box, and wipe the stage and pads with a damp tissue to pick up slivers. Check the microscope is still on its tape. Nothing is used up.
fidelity: Rigid PhysX at 400 Hz, 20 Hz control. The slide is one 4.7 g body of three boxes (label end, specimen part, 0.2 mm coverslip); contact points and normals tell edge from face touches. GPU PhysX has no CCD; 400 Hz stands in. Cracking is not simulated: face contact, objective contact and a hard landing are rules. The caliper is a revolute arm on a torsion spring (1.5 N at the tip, est.); the stage is two prismatic axes with stick-slip friction (5 N breakaway, est.); frame and optics are static.
